item.title: More from Fed’s Bowman: Shifts focus to inflation, wants AI and Middle East risks to ease first
item.description:
Overall the comments lean hawkish. Bowman’s shift in focus to inflation and her link to Middle East risk keep energy prices at the centre of the Fed debate, which supports the US dollar and front-end Treasury yields. Her emphasis on pace and timeline suggests a preference for gradual tightening rather than aggressive moves, which may temper any repricing toward bigger or faster hikes. For gold, a firmer case for further tightening has been a headwind during this conflict, not a support. Oil traders may read her remarks as a reminder that any further Middle East escalation now feeds directly into Fed policy risk.

---

Earlier:

  • Fed's Bowman: Persistent inflation, firming labor conditions suggest 'work to do'

---

Bowman has turned firmly toward the inflation fight, but her talk of pace and timeline suggests she would rather take it step by step than rush.

Summary:

  • Bowman said she is shifting her focus to inflation and that its lack of a downward trend should give the Fed pause
  • She would need to see AI and Middle East risks fade before she could be confident inflation will fall next year
  • Longer-term inflation expectations are very well anchored, she said, but they do not necessarily drive her thinking
  • She said the Fed needs to consider the pace and timeline of its response, citing last year’s gradual cuts, pause and resumption as a model
  • She does not expect AI to cost the US economy jobs overall, and sees productivity gains and new roles instead
  • On supervision, she expects to finalise the GSIB surcharge and Basel III rules in the coming weeks, with her focus moving to smaller-bank rules

Federal Reserve Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman said she is shifting her focus to inflation, arguing that the lack of a downward trend in price pressures should give policymakers pause. She added that she would need to see risks tied to artificial intelligence and the Middle East fade before she could be confident inflation will come down next year.

The remarks, made in a question-and-answer session on Tuesday, followed earlier comments in which Bowman said persistent inflation and firming labour market conditions suggest the Fed still has work to do. In those remarks, she estimated that core PCE inflation likely ran at 3.3% in October, driven by energy prices and AI-related demand.

Her latest comments were more mixed in tone. On one side, Bowman said longer-term inflation expectations remain very well anchored. She called expectations an important data point but said they do not necessarily drive her thinking, which suggests anchored expectations alone will not settle her policy view.

On the other side, she said the Fed needs to think about the pace and timeline for addressing inflation. She drew a parallel with the central bank’s approach last year, when it cut rates gradually, paused, and then resumed. In her view, a similarly measured, step-by-step approach could be used to tackle inflation in the coming months. That framing points to a preference for gradual tightening over a rapid move, rather than signalling any specific decision.

On the labour market, Bowman said she does not expect AI to rob the US economy of jobs. She expects the technology to make workers more productive, create new roles and remove less necessary ones.

Bowman also covered her supervisory brief. She said she hopes and expects to finalise rules on the surcharge for global systemically important banks (GSIBs) and on Basel III capital standards in the coming weeks, and that her attention has turned to rules and supervisory approaches for smaller banks. She noted that the Fed carries out ongoing cybersecurity examinations of banks and has seen a strong focus on finding and patching vulnerabilities. She also said open lines of communication with the Treasury are critically important.

Taken together, the comments keep the inflation fight at the centre of Bowman’s thinking, while her emphasis on pace suggests she favours a measured path. Upcoming inflation data, and any easing in energy and AI-related price pressures, will be key to how far that view moves.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: investingLive Americas FX news wrap 10 Nov: It’s a Wrap. Hot US CPI puts a bigger Fed hike in play
item.description:
• US stock market close: Hot CPI leads to a selloff
  • Fed's Bowman: Persistent inflation, firming labor conditions suggest 'work to do'
  • Nvidia falls another 6% and is now testing a key support zone
  • Fed's Schmid: Some concerning trends in prices, underneath the whole energy story
  • Bank of Canada minutes: Governing Council sees possible need to hike rates further
  • U.S. Treasury sells $42 billion of 10 year notes at a high yield of 5.02%
  • ECB’s Lane says the bar for directional rate guidance is high
  • European stocks mostly higher as hot US CPI sends Treasury yields above 5%
  • Iran's Rezaei: No negotiations currently taking place between Tehran and Washington
  • Bitcoin tests its 200 day moving average after hotter US CPI data
  • Fed's Logan: It's clear that Fed needs at least two more quarter-point rate hikes
  • US 2-year yields surge as the market realizes the US has an inflation problem
  • US October core CPI +0.3% vs +0.2% expected
  • Morning Kickstart. Oil slides as Waller puts a half-point hike in play. Markets brace for CPI
  • investingLive European news wrap: Fed's Waller floats case for 50 bps hike in December

October CPI was the story. Headline inflation slowed from September, but both headline and core prices rose more than expected. The core reading mattered most. Before the release, Fed Governor Christopher Waller had flagged a 0.3% reading as the point where a larger December hike could come into play. That’s what the report showed at published precision, and traders raised the odds of a half-point move. images.investinglive.com.  The current numbers put a 50 bp hike in December at 10% while a 25 bp hike is the other 90%.  

The 2-year yield led the move higher, the dollar gained against every major currency in the late-session snapshot, and gold and silver fell. Anthropic’s IPO terms gave tech stocks an early lift, but the Nasdaq Composite ended the session snapshot down 0.74%. investinglive.com

The dollar rises across the board

The dollar gained the most against the Australian dollar, with AUDUSD down 0.91% to 0.6863, followed by a 0.75% decline in GBPUSD to 1.3339. EURUSD fell 0.55% to 1.1161, while USDJPY rose 0.55% to 158.77 (see technical post here). The dollar’s smallest gain was against the Canadian dollar, with USDCAD up 0.51% to 1.4189.

Treasury yields jump, led by the 2-year

  • 2-year yield 4.7335%, +18.65 basis points
  • 5-year yield 4.8121%, +15.31 basis points
  • 10-year yield 4.9875%, +12.55 basis points
  • 30-year yield 5.3502%, +9.42 basis points

The 10-year traded above 5% during the session and was back just below it in the late snapshot. The bigger move in the 2-year tells the story. Traders were repricing what the Fed might do over the next few meetings. A soft $42 billion 10-year auction added to the pressure. It stopped at 5.02%, 1 basis point above the when-issued yield, and the 2.46x bid-to-cover ratio fell short of the 2.60x average. Strong direct demand only partly offset weaker indirect demand and a larger dealer takedown. investinglive.com

US stocks give back the Anthropic bounce

Late-session levels from the supplied snapshot

  • Dow industrial average 52,237.23, −0.30%
  • S&P 500 7,520.93, −0.38%
  • Nasdaq Composite 20,065.87, −0.74%
  • Russell 2000 2,821.38, −0.68%
  • Nasdaq 100 27,740.80, −0.60%

Anthropic’s IPO gives tech a lift that fades

Anthropic kicked off its IPO roadshow with updated terms after retracting preliminary figures sent to bankers. The Claude maker and selling shareholders are offering 825 million shares at $70 to $78 each, for a deal worth up to $64.4 billion and an implied valuation of up to $1.4 trillion. The shares are expected to start trading on Nasdaq on November 19 under the ticker ANT. investinglive.com

Reports that orders covered the available shares helped push the Nasdaq indices into positive territory earlier in the session. The bounce faded. Demand for the offering is one barometer of investors’ appetite for AI, while today’s jump in yields raised the hurdle for growth-stock valuations across the market. investinglive.com

European stocks mostly higher, led by Spain

  • Spain’s IBEX 35 +0.98%
  • Italy’s FTSE MIB +0.69%
  • France’s CAC 40 +0.55%
  • Germany’s DAX +0.31%
  • UK’s FTSE 100 −0.29%. investinglive.com

US CPI. Headline slows, but core stays sticky

Headline CPI rose 0.4% in October versus 0.3% expected and 0.6% in September. Core CPI rose 0.3% versus 0.2% expected, the third straight month at 0.3% on a rounded basis. The BLS had no October 2025 comparison because of last year’s government shutdown, so the October report came without year-over-year readings. September’s annual rates were 3.7% for headline and 2.6% for core.

Energy rose 0.7% after September’s 5.2% jump, helping explain the slowdown in headline CPI. Shelter rose 0.3% and accounted for more than 30% of the headline increase. Food rose 0.5%. Under the surface, motor vehicle insurance rose 0.7% and airfares climbed 0.4%, while used-car prices fell 1.2%. InvestingLive put core services excluding shelter, often called supercore, at roughly 0.4% for the month.

The distinction for the Fed is that the energy impulse cooled sharply while core inflation held its pace. The unrounded core reading was 0.297%, close enough to Waller’s 0.3% marker to get the market’s attention. October PCE and November payrolls are still due before the December meeting. PCE is the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, and payrolls will help show how much room the Fed has to tighten. images.investinglive.com

The Fed speakers, one by one

A number of Fed speakers did talk today and they were more hawkish him

Christopher Waller. Speaking before CPI, Waller said he would support a 25-basis-point December hike even if October inflation improved. He opened the door to a 50-basis-point move if core CPI came in at 0.3% or higher. He sees the labor market as broadly balanced and is concerned about how widely price increases have spread, including whether higher energy costs are feeding into other goods and services.

Michelle Bowman. Speaking after the release, Bowman said the CPI report suggested inflation pressures could persist longer and that labor-market conditions appeared to be firming. She pointed to October PCE and November payrolls as two inputs still to come before the December decision. She also wants to assess how durable AI-related demand is and how geopolitical risks feed through to the economy.

Jeff Schmid. The Kansas City Fed president called current policy fairly accommodative. Housing stood out as an area where rates may be biting, but he saw little evidence of restraint elsewhere. He also flagged concerning price trends beneath the energy headlines. His argument was that the current rate setting is doing too little to slow inflation. images.investinglive.com

Lorie Logan. The Dallas Fed president said she sees a need for at least two more quarter-point hikes and that the Fed may be able to move faster this winter. After those two moves, she would see a case for pausing to assess the economy. She also said higher bond yields signal that monetary policy still has work to do.

The overall message. All four put inflation front and center, but they emphasized different parts of the decision. Waller put the size of the December move in play. Logan laid out a path of at least two more increases. Schmid questioned whether current policy is restrictive enough, and Bowman emphasized the data still to come. The jump in the 2-year yield was the clearest sign that traders took the prospect of faster tightening seriously.

Oil slips. Metals and crypto fall harder.

WTI was down 0.56% at $86.36 after trading as low as $83.88, while Brent slipped 0.67% to $91.95. Hopes for progress in US–Iran talks remained in the background. Today’s softer crude prices offered some relief on energy costs, but the bond market took its cue from the CPI surprise and the Fed’s response. investinglive.com

Gold fell 2.59% to around $4,032 and silver dropped 3.54% to $51.52. A stronger dollar and higher Treasury yields were headwinds for both. Bitcoin fell 1.42% to around $73,881, moving in the same direction as growth stocks, while Ethereum lost 3.18% to $2,059.42.

The 2-year yield is the barometer going forward. October CPI brought a larger December hike into the conversation. The next test is whether October PCE confirms the persistence in core prices and whether November payrolls give the Fed room to move faster. investing.com

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Costco declares $30 special dividend worth $13.3 billion, renews $4 billion buyback
item.description:
A $30 payout goes well past the roughly $24 per share that analysts had estimated would match the yield of the 2024 special dividend, so it is likely to be read as a positive surprise on size, not just timing. In the past, Costco shares have firmed in the days after a special dividend is announced, as investors buy in to qualify before the record date. The bigger question for valuation is balance-sheet strength: returning $13.3 billion in one go uses a large share of the cash the company has built up. Over time, the renewed buyback also gives Costco more room to support the share count.

---

Earlier:

  • CoreWeave Q3 beats on seven key metrics, lifts full-year revenue and run-rate guidance

---

Costco has delivered the special dividend shareholders were waiting for, and at $30 a share it is twice the size of the last one.

Summary:

  • Costco declared a special cash dividend of $30 per share, worth about $13.3 billion in total
  • Payable December 4 to shareholders of record at the close of business on November 24
  • New $4 billion share repurchase program approved, running to November 2030
  • It replaces a $4 billion plan from 2023, due to expire in January 2027, under which $3.1 billion had been bought back
  • The payout is double the $15 special dividend paid in January 2024

Costco Wholesale (COST) has declared a special cash dividend of $30 per share, a one-off payout worth about $13.3 billion in total. It has also approved a new $4 billion share repurchase program, the company said in a statement on November 10.

The special dividend is payable on December 4 to shareholders of record at the close of business on November 24. It is paid on top of Costco’s regular quarterly dividend.

The new buyback authorisation runs until November 2030. It replaces a $4 billion program adopted in 2023 and due to expire in January 2027, under which the company had bought back $3.1 billion of stock. That leaves roughly $900 million of capacity unused on the old plan as it is retired.

This is the largest special dividend in Costco’s history, double the $15 per share it paid in January 2024. The retailer has made such payments every few years since 2012, usually funding them from cash on hand rather than borrowing, and shareholders had been watching for the next one.

Management had flagged the possibility. Chief Financial Officer Gary Millerchip said earlier this year that at the company’s current valuation, a special dividend is typically the most effective way to return excess cash while keeping the flexibility to invest in growth. He also noted that with the share price well above its level at the last payout, a larger cash pile would be needed to deliver a similar yield. Analysts had estimated that matching the roughly 2.4% yield of the 2024 dividend would take around $24 per share, so the $30 figure goes beyond that benchmark.

Costco’s statement did not say how the dividend or the buyback would be funded, and it included no executive commentary. The company operates 945 warehouses, 653 of them in the United States and Puerto Rico, and runs e-commerce sites in nine countries.

For shareholders, the key date is November 24, when investors must be on the register to qualify. Under standard US settlement, the shares are expected to go ex-dividend on or around that date. With this much cash going out, attention is likely to turn to how quickly Costco rebuilds its balance sheet and whether it uses the renewed buyback more actively than the last one.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: CoreWeave Q3 beats on seven key metrics, lifts full-year revenue and run-rate guidance
item.description:
A clean beat plus a guidance raise gives CoreWeave bulls the combination they look for, and it adds support to the wider AI infrastructure trade. The margin beat is the strongest signal for sentiment because it answers concerns that rapid capacity growth comes at the expense of profitability. Traders will look past the headline beat to the size of the guidance upgrade, since the raised ranges were not disclosed in the initial results. Any read-through to AI compute demand could carry over to chipmakers and data-centre names during the next US session.

---

CoreWeave beat on every line, with margins leading the way, and then raised its outlook, which puts the focus on just how large the upgrade is.

Summary:

  • Q3 revenue of around $3.7 billion, ahead of estimates near $3.6 billion
  • Loss of $1.27 per share against an expected loss of $1.46; net loss of about $710 million versus roughly $850 million expected
  • Operating income of about $207 million, more than three times the roughly $64 million forecast; adjusted operating income of around $380 million versus about $246 million
  • Adjusted EBITDA of about $2.3 billion versus around $2.05 billion expected, with a 62% margin against roughly 58% forecast
  • Full-year 2026 revenue guidance and annualised run-rate revenue guidance both raised

CoreWeave (CRWV) reported third-quarter results that beat analyst expectations on every headline measure, and the AI cloud infrastructure provider raised both its full-year 2026 revenue guidance and its annualised run-rate revenue guidance.

Revenue came in at around $3.7 billion, ahead of consensus estimates near $3.6 billion. The company posted a loss of $1.27 per share, narrower than the $1.46 loss analysts had pencilled in. Its net loss of roughly $710 million compared with expectations of about $850 million.

The bigger surprise came higher up the income statement. Operating income reached about $207 million, more than three times the roughly $64 million that analysts had forecast. On an adjusted basis, operating income was around $380 million against estimates near $246 million. Adjusted EBITDA came in at about $2.3 billion versus expectations of around $2.05 billion, and the adjusted EBITDA margin of 62% was well above the roughly 58% analysts had expected.

The gap between the operating figures and the bottom line is worth noting. CoreWeave is profitable at the operating level and generates large adjusted EBITDA, yet it still reports a net loss. In a capital-heavy business of this kind, that gap usually reflects depreciation on hardware and the cost of financing. Investors are likely to keep weighing margin strength against the cost of funding growth.

Even so, the quarter points to improving operating leverage. Beating the margin estimate by more than four percentage points suggests revenue is growing faster than the costs of delivering it. That is the central test for an infrastructure provider that is scaling up capacity.

The guidance upgrades may matter more than the beat itself. Raising both the full-year revenue outlook and the annualised run-rate forecast signals that management is confident demand for AI computing capacity will hold up through the end of the year. The headline results did not include the new guidance ranges, so the size of the upgrade compared with market expectations will be a key focus.

Investors will next look for the detail behind the raised outlook on the earnings call: the revised revenue ranges, and any comments on capacity, customer demand and capital spending plans. 

---

CoreWeave, based in New Jersey, rents out large-scale computing power built on Nvidia graphics processors to companies that train and run AI models. It started out as a crypto mining company, moved into serving AI and high-performance computing customers, and rebranded as CoreWeave in 2021. It listed on Nasdaq in March 2025, raising about $1.5 billion. Its largest contracts are with major tech and AI companies. OpenAI has committed roughly $22.4 billion, Meta about $14.2 billion through 2031, and Microsoft has historically accounted for around 70% of annual revenue. In April, Meta signed a further deal worth about $21 billion, running through 2032. Nvidia is both CoreWeave’s chip supplier and an investor in the company, and it invested another $2 billion in January 2026.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: US stock market close: Hot CPI leads to a selloff
item.description:
US equity futures were flat ahead of the CPI report but plunged afterwards. Fed Governor Waller set the stage for a drop when he said a reading of +0.3% on core inflation would make him consider at 50 basis point hike in December.

So when CPI was +0.3% with some caveats that could have made it higher (like a -1.2% m/m drop in used car prices) that sent a shudder through the market. US 2-year yields jump 18 bps and 10s rose above above 5%. In turn, stock markets were under pressure.

Notably, the selling was mostly contained to tech as the AI angst continues. Nvidia was down another 6% as politicians target Nvidia's chip sales to China in light of the honeypot revelation. The whole bit feels a bit scripted but that's the name of the game in Washington.  There were some decent pockets of strength and breadth was relatively balanced. Notably, there was a nice pop when it was revealed that Anthropic already has a full order book for next week's $60 billion IPO.

There was a real ebb and flow to the day but the bulls gathered themselves late for a decent close that erased much of the pain.

Closing changes:

  • S&P 500 -0.4%
  • Nasdaq Comp -0.7%
  • DJIA -0.3%
  • Russell 2000 -0.8%
  • TSX Comp -0.8%

Note that US stock markets are open on Wednesday for Veteran's Day but Canadian markets and US bond markets are closed. The lack of activity from US fixed income should keep a lid on volatiltiy but we're waiting for earnings from neocloud CoreWeave after the bell so that will be a big driver.

item.title: Intel bounces from $51.50 swing area support. Can buyers build on it?
item.description:
Recall that in August 2025, the Trump administration announced an $8.9 billion deal for a 9.9% stake in Intel. The agreement covered up to 433.3 million shares at an announced average price of $20.47, as part of a push to strengthen domestic chip manufacturing and national security.

When Intel reached $142.35 in early July, those 433.3 million shares would have been worth about $61.7 billion. That was a paper gain of roughly $52.8 billion, or 595%, in less than a year.  However, share momentum faded, chips got hammered and Intell was one of the stocks which led the decline. 

At the current level of $57.70, the same share count implies a value of about $25 billion and a paper gain of roughly $16.1 billion, or 182%. That’s still a sizable gain, but it is. also about $36.7 billion below the peak valuation. Easy come, easy go.

Old resistance gets a test as support

So given the sharp declines from the peak, what are the technicals telling traders at $57.70? More specifically, "Is it time to buy?"

Last week’s selloff took shares of Intel down to $51.50. That was also near the December 2023 swing high at the same level. The stock didn’t get above that old high until January 21, 2026, when it reached $54.47. It then corrected toward $41 before breaking above $54.47 on April 8 2026 and running to $142.35 about three months later.

The swing low from 2023 and the swing high from 2026, makes $51.50–$54.47 the swing area to watch (see the yellow are on the chart above). Sellers pushed below the upper edge last week but ran out of momentum near the lower edge ($51.50). The subsequent bounce back above $54.47 gives buyers a foothold. If the price slips back into the area, $51.50 becomes the key barometer for risk again. Move below it is more bearish, and buyers should get out.  Stay above it and the buyers are in play and hoping upside momentum begins again.

What are the upside targets?

So the question traders can ask is what are the upside targets if they buy at the discounted levels?

Looking at the chart:

  • $66.21 is the broken 61.8% retracement of the rally from the August 2025 low to the July 2026 high. It’s the first upside target, $8.51 above he current level at $57.70.

  • Above that and $80.75 is the 50% midpoint of that same move. Getting and staying above $66.21 would open the door toward that level, $23.05 above $57.70.

What is the risk?

From $57.70, the close risk level is last week’s low at $51.50, a distance of $6.20 per share. Using the round natural support at the $50 level gives the trade more room and puts the distance and risk at $7.70 per share. That’s as much room as I’d give this setup. If the price goes below that level, there could be more trader liquidation.  

Using $51.50 as the risk level, the first target offers about 1.4 times the risk. The midpoint offers about 3.7 times the risk, but buyers have to get through $66.21 first.

Is it something you would do?  Smart traders look at the risk and evaluated to the return.  

Education. Why lean against an old swing high?

When a stock breaks above an old high, traders often watch that same level on a pullback to see whether buyers will defend it. Intel gave us that test near $51.50. The bounce tells us buyers showed up there. A break below last week’s low would take away the reason for leaning against that support in the first place.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Fed's Bowman: Persistent inflation, firming labor conditions suggest 'work to do'
item.description:
• Persistent inflation, firming labor conditions suggest ‘still work to do’
  • Financial conditions have tightened, Fed must weigh costs of additional policy tightening
  • Bringing inflation down remains a priority
  • Core PCE likely rose 3.3% in October on energy prices, AI-related demand
  • As shocks unwind, forecast core PCE to move closer to 2% next year
  • Economic growth gained momentum this year
  • CPI data suggests inflation pressures may persist
  • Labor market has improved, not tight, not adding to inflation

It's funny how all the people who turned to doves in order to bid for the Fed Chair nomination are now pivoting back to being hawks because their party lost the midterms in large part due to deteriorating affordability.

Overall, she hasn't performed the full 360, back into the hawk she started out as, but she's moving in that direction. The body of the remarks is still laced with off-ramps: labor isn’t adding to inflation, shocks will unwind on their own, core PCE drifts toward 2% next year, and — the real tell — financial conditions have tightened enough that the Fed “must weigh the costs” of going further.

That’s the language of someone who’ll vote for the next hike reluctantly and look for the exit the next time stock markets gap down. Note the direct contradiction with Logan on labor: Bowman says improved-not-tight, Logan says balanced-and-tightening. That’s a committee split on the output gap itself, not just tactics. With 27.7 bps priced this year, Bowman neither confirms nor fights it, but she’s the clearest signal yet that the hiking bloc isn’t monolithic.

I have a hard time taking any of them seriously on the inflation front right now after they all just opted to hold when oil was $15 higher.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nvidia falls another 6% and is now testing a key support zone
item.description:
Shares of Nvidia are in the penalty box as the market tries to figure out what will happen with CEO Jensen Huang.

The company founder appears to have been caught in a Chinese honeypot as he admitted to an affair with a woman who US officials said was passing on information to Beijing. I have my doubts that this story would have played out the same way if it weren't politically motivated. This is information that would likely have been passed onto him privately, rather than discovered by the media.

The problem is: That's even worse. 

My guess is this was leaked in order to further a political agenda and the timing right after the midterms supports that. The likely goal is to further cut down on Chinese connections to Nvidia chips, as Huang was adamantly opposed to chip curbs to China. The thinking is that he facilitated back doors to those sales or to vendors who would allow for virtual access, or that he turned a blind eye to it.

It's highly unlikely that he could have told a spy anything that China didn't already know about the manufacturing process so the problem now is that he's in a battle with the US government. You can see how that looks on the chart, as it's now right up against support from the March 2026 and Sept 2025 lows.

A break here might target the Nov 2024 high near $153, or even lower.

What Nvidia has going for it is valuation. It now trades at 21x trailign P/E, 18x forward P/E and 10.5x consensus 2028 earnings. If you're bullish on AI, those are interesting numbers. Obviously, there is plenty of disruption coming on the chip side but Nvidia has opportunities of its own to disrupt things like self-driving cars, robotics and frontier models.

Huang likely tried to bullet the US government on AI and is now finding out that's a losing battle. He will surely retreat but all indications is that he's still a founder with an intense fire in his belly who wants to win the AI race. I would be a shame if he departed.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Anthropic looks to be pricing its IPO for success
item.description:
There are two kinds of IPOs.

Most recently, all the high-profile IPOs have been cash-outs. They have been vehicles for venture capitalists to hype up an offering at a ridiculous valuation and use retail for exit liquidity. CNBC plays into this by giving wall-to-wall coverage to IPOs, despite years of them costing retail traders money, particularly the ones they have focused intensely on.

On the other side are IPOs for companies that are looking to build a long-term shareholder base. In those, the IPO isn't priced overly aggressively and the fundraising isn't too high.

Anthropic is showing signs that it wants to be in the latter camp. Reports today say they have already found bids for $60 billion, which is the reported size of the IPO. It wasn't disclosed what the price on that will be, but it's likely to creep higher as we get close to the finish line. In any case, it doesn't look like they're trying to maximize the valuation at this point. There was talk of $2 trillion earlier this year and now it looks to be in the $1.25 to $1.75 trillion range.

Now I'm not going to argue that isn't a huge number and the whole thing requires some heroic assumptions but the adjustments on the valuation don't scream that this is one to avoid.

The FT reports that Goldman Sachs, the lead bank on the deal, is telling investors Anthropic will do about $52 billion in revenue this year, up from $4.6 billion in 2025. More than 10x is always good.

From there the forecast is $136 billion in 2027, $442 billion in 2029 and more than $600 billion in 2030.

Put that in perspective. Only two companies in the S&P 500 have revenue above $600 billion: Amazon and Walmart, both a little over $700 billion. Apple is at $416 billion. Goldman is saying a company founded less than six years ago will be the third-largest in America by sales in four years.

On those numbers, the valuation math changes quickly. At $1.25 to $1.75 trillion, you’re paying 24 to 34 times this year’s revenue, which is nosebleed territory. On the 2027 number it’s 9 to 13 times. On 2030 it’s 2 to 3 times, which is cheaper than the S&P 500 trades today. I'm very skeptical but skepticism hasn't exactly paid in the AI boom.

There is also a catch, and it’s a big one. Goldman doesn’t see Anthropic turning free cash flow positive until 2030, when it forecasts $33.6 billion. That’s a margin under 6% on $600 billion in sales, and it puts the IPO at 37 to 52 times free cash flow that’s four years away. Meanwhile, the company has committed to spend around $900 billion on computing capacity. The $60 billion raise is a rounding error against that bill.

Remember who is making these forecasts too. This is the bank selling the deal, talking to a potential buyer. Revenue has to grow 160% next year and then keep compounding at 80% a year through 2029 just to hit the script.

That's not the kind of thing that gets me excited and I will not be even thinking about buying the opening print but -- for the broader market -- there are indications it will go well.

item.title: Bank of Canada minutes: Governing Council sees possible need to hike rates further
item.description:
• Governing Council deliberated two options: hold at 2.25% or hike to 2.50%
  • Members agreed there “could be a need to increase the policy rate further”
  • Decisions will be taken “one meeting at a time”
  • Risk that high inflation persists and becomes broad-based has increased
  • Higher-for-longer oil scenario from the April MPR has “unfortunately come to pass”
  • Oil is about US$35 above the July MPR assumption
  • Even without pass-through, the energy shock alone keeps CPI around 3% for more than a year
  • CPI seen at 3.5% at the end of 2026 and above 3% through much of 2027; back to 2% by mid-2028
  • Core measures remain near 2%; CPI ex-gasoline at 2.2%
  • Cost pass-through limited so far, but members agreed it will eventually hit consumer prices
  • Members had a “diversity of views” on the speed and extent of pass-through
  • Near-term inflation expectations have moved up; longer-term expectations remain anchored
  • Downside risks to inflation have diminished since July
  • Some slack remains; unemployment rate around 6.5%
  • Some members see the labour market as stronger than the headline numbers suggest
  • 2026 growth revised up to 1%; 2% in 2027 and 2028
  • Uncertainty “did not mean inaction”

It was a pre-emptive hike, and the minutes don’t hide it. Core inflation is near 2%, CPI ex-gasoline is 2.2% and unemployment is stuck around 6.5%. That’s not the profile of an economy that needs tighter policy. The Bank of Canada hiked anyway because Tiff Macklem is a general fighting the last war.

The key line is that the energy shock alone keeps CPI near 3% for more than a year, even with zero pass-through. Add in businesses telling the BOC they plan to pass on more costs and you get a central bank that has stopped looking through oil. Eight months into the war, “transitory” isn’t an argument anyone wants to make.

That said, this isn’t a central bank on autopilot. The case for holding was real, trade talks with the US have broken down and business sentiment has soured. The next move depends on oil and and that has a silver lining as it's fallen fast. However, if core CPI ticks higher in the next two reports, December is live. If it doesn’t, they can afford to wait.

item.title: European stocks mostly higher as hot US CPI sends Treasury yields above 5%
item.description:
As London and European traders head home for the day, the major continental indices are mostly higher, with Spain leading the way. The UK’s FTSE 100 went the other way. In the US, the stronger-than-expected CPI report is still driving the bond and currency markets. The 10-year Treasury yield is back above 5%, the dollar is higher across the board, and an early Nasdaq rebound on Anthropic IPO news has given way to renewed selling.

Spain leads European stocks higher. The FTSE 100 lags.

Spain’s IBEX 35 rose 0.98%, followed by Italy’s FTSE MIB at +0.69%, France’s CAC 40 at +0.55% and Germany’s DAX at +0.31%. The UK’s FTSE 100 fell 0.29%.

European benchmark yields moved higher across the board. France’s 10-year led the move, up 8.5 basis points to 4.806%. Germany rose 7.5 basis points to 3.328%, Spain and Italy each rose 7.4 basis points to 3.896% and 4.380%, respectively, and the UK rose 6.8 basis points to 5.208%.

Hotter US CPI pushes the 10-year back above 5%

October headline CPI rose 0.4% versus 0.3% expected, while core CPI rose 0.3% versus 0.2% expected. Headline inflation slowed from September’s 0.6%, but core matched the prior month. On a three-month annualized basis, headline CPI was running at 5.7% and core at 3.7%. The upside surprises gave traders another reason to price in tighter Fed policy after Governor Christopher Waller raised the possibility of a 50-basis-point hike in December.

The US 2-year yield was up 21.4 basis points to 4.761%, the 5-year was up 18.4 basis points to 4.843%, and the 10-year was up 15.5 basis points to 5.017%. The 30-year rose 11.9 basis points to 5.375%. For the rest of the US session, 5% is the barometer for the 10-year. The next thing to watch is whether yields can hold above it.

Waller put 0.3% core CPI in focus before the release

Speaking in London before the CPI report, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said he was leaning toward a 25-basis-point hike in December even if inflation cooled in October. If core CPI came in around 0.3% or higher, he said the Fed should consider 50 basis points. His reasoning was that the economy was still growing at a solid pace, the labor market was stable, and inflation was broad enough that moving too slowly could put the Fed’s credibility at risk. Core CPI came in at 0.3%, right around the level he had flagged. That helps explain why the 2-year yield led the move higher, jumping more than 21 basis points to 4.76% by the European close.

Waller also made a point that ties into today’s drop in crude. Oil can fall on hopes for de-escalation in the Middle East, but he said limited refining capacity could keep diesel prices elevated even as crude gets cheaper. For the Fed, the question is how much of those higher energy costs are still feeding through to the prices of other goods and services.

Anthropic gives the Nasdaq a lift, but the gains fade

The Nasdaq indices erased their early losses and briefly moved into positive territory after reports that Anthropic is targeting November 18 to price its IPO and November 19 for its trading debut. Reports indicated that orders already covered the available shares and that roughly 20% of the offering could go to retail investors.

By the European close, the Nasdaq Composite was back down 1.21% and the Nasdaq 100 was down 1.22%. The Dow was down 0.56%, the S&P 500 was down 0.77%, and the Russell 2000 was down 1.18%.

The dollar extends its gains. Gold and silver slide.

EURUSD was down 0.65% at 1.1150 and GBPUSD was down 0.86% at 1.3325. Both pairs moved back below their 200-hour moving averages after CPI. Those averages now give sellers a nearby level to lean against. USDJPY was up 0.56% at 158.79, near its session high of 158.84. AUDUSD was down 1.08% at 0.6851, the largest decline among the major currencies in the snapshot.

Gold was down 2.8% near $4,023 and silver was down 3.9% near $51.32 as yields and the dollar moved higher. Bitcoin was down about 2.6% near $73,020.

Crude oil remains lower, but buyers return from below $84

WTI was down $0.31 at $86.54 after trading as low as $83.88. That puts it $2.66 off the low and within $0.39 of the session high at $86.93. Brent was down $0.64 at $91.93 after dipping to $89.16.

On the Middle East front, President Trump played down the prospect of renewed major strikes against Iran after meeting with Qatar’s prime minister on Monday. Secretary of State Marco Rubio reinforced that message on Tuesday, saying the administration saw less need for major combat operations while sanctions and the naval blockade remained in place. Iran’s top security official said no negotiations with Washington were underway, and the Strait of Hormuz remained a sticking point. The softer US tone helped take some of the supply risk premium out of crude early, but both benchmarks had recovered much of their losses by the European close.

item.title: US 2-year yields surge as the market realizes the US has an inflation problem
item.description:
The bond market is kicking and screaming again.

US 2-year yields are up 19 basis points to 4.73% as the market digests a hut CPI report and comments from Chris Waller. The Fed Governor said that a 50 basis points hike was on the table for December if core CPI ran at +0.3% or higher. Well it was at 0.3% and if not for a 1.2% drop in monthly used auto prices, then it would have been +0.4%. Waller also highlighted the widening breadth of price increases and that was evident in the report.

This month, the market had grown less worried about inflation because oil prices have fallen but the Fed thinking is that inflationary expectations are starting to get built into 2027 price setting. That's something I highlighted in late October, as Whirlpool said it would hike price 7% starting December 3.

The Fed was wrong when it said that tariff effects would move through the economy quickly and now we're seeing that. Companies like Whirlpool saw margins collapse and tried to avoid price hikes. Consumers had also benchmarked on lower prices and some income segments are certainly struggling but eventually vendors realize they have to hike prices as the costs of things like steel and other inputs move through the supply chain.

I think the Fed is getting that rude awakening right now. Oil prices have obviously come down but product cracks are stiill absurdly wide so that limits the downside for now. I can't see that materially improving unless we get peace in the Middle East and Ukraine. There have been some positive steps recently but there's no sign a concluded deal on either front is imminent, so I'd argue that risks are towards sentiment worsening.

Here is what Marco Rubio, the US Secretary of State, said today:

At the moment, the talks have not been particularly productive because the Iranian demands are simply unacceptable, and in some cases they are outrageous, ridiculous, and detached from reality... We're not going to pay. Iran, you know, is demanding reparations. They should be the ones paying reparations because they're the ones that have, you know, destabilized the region for long periods of time. They're demanding pallets of cash, which the president made clear is not going to happen. If they want a nuclear energy program, they should have one, like many other countries around the world have. So there's things they can do, but just right now they just don't seem, you know, at that point. Now I think they want a deal. There's no doubt they'd like a deal too, but they're just not ready to make one apparently. But we're open to a little bit changes. But I don't think status quo is the right way to phrase this. Status quo means that things are going to stay static. They're not. They're going to continue to grow. What I'm saying to you is that the economic campaign is so devastating that right now there really is no need for major combat operations. The president has basically said that over the last few days, and that's what I told our European allies today.

That doesn't sound great.

So as the election dust settles, it's starting to look like nothing will change and that's problematic and inflationary. I would also argue that at some point you will have to price in a Democratic sweep in 2028 and all the fiscal largess that will come with it, if Republicans don't force some kind of strategy change on Iran or tariffs.

  • Medical care: +0.3% vs +0.1% prior
  • Lodging away from home: +0.6% vs +2.0% prior
  • Energy m/m: +0.7% vs +5.2% prior
  • Gasoline m/m: +1.0% vs +9.1% prior
  • Food m/m: +0.5% vs 0.0% prior
  • New vehicles: +0.2% vs +0.2% prior

Note that the BLS did not collect survey data for October 2025 because of a lapse in appropriations during the government shutdown. That also makes many of the numbers impossible to calculate.

Summing the BLS contribution table (food 0.064, energy 0.053, core 0.234) gives about +0.35% unrounded, which makes the headline number a tad better than it looks.

Following Waller's hawkish comments, the market is fully priced for a December hike and is pricing in 60 bps of hiking in the year ahead. USD/JPY was trading at 158.19 ahead of the data and 158.44 afterawrds. S&P 500 futures were flat but down 0.7% afterwards. US 2-year yields were up 9 bps ahead of the data and +13 bps afterwards.

Waller said a half-point hike might be needed in December if core CPI comes in "around 0.3% or higher". That raised the stakes on today's report. He also said, he would support quarter-point rate hike in December even if October CPI improves versus September. Notably, he said he was particularly concerned about the breadth of price increases.

Looking through the data, the breadth shows up in supercore at +0.4%. Used cars and communications were “among the small number of major indexes that decreased," the BLS wrote. Core goods ex-used cars rose 0.4% and core ex-shelter and used cars rose 0.4%, both the largest since January. Used car prices fell 1.2% m/m in October and without that, this report would have been ugly at +0.4% in all the key metrics instead of +0.3%.

Furnishings and supplies rose 0.7%, the largest since June 2025. Furniture was +1.2%, appliances +1.3%, tools and hardware +1.4%, and housekeeping supplies +0.9% (largest since January 2023). Transportation services were up 0.8%, the largest since January. Insurance was +0.7%, maintenance and repair +0.6%, and public transportation +2.0%.

For background, the Consumer Price Index from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics is the most market-moving inflation report in the world. It’s released monthly at 8:30 am ET, usually in the second week of the following month, and measures changes in the prices urban consumers pay for a basket of goods and services, including food, energy, shelter, vehicles, apparel, medical care, transportation and recreation.

Unlike Canada, where the focus is the unadjusted annual rate, US markets zero in on the seasonally adjusted monthly change, particularly in core CPI, which excludes food and energy. Traders often calculate the unrounded figures from the index levels, because the difference between a 0.24% and a 0.26% monthly gain can decide whether the print rounds up or down and how markets react.

Shelter is the largest component, at roughly a third of the overall index. It’s dominated by owners’ equivalent rent, an estimate of what homeowners would pay to rent their own homes, along with rent of primary residence. Because shelter is measured through leases that turn over slowly, it lags market rents by many months.

Markets also watch supercore inflation, core services excluding housing, which is seen as the best gauge of wage-driven price pressures. Volatile categories such as airfares, used cars, motor vehicle insurance and lodging away from home frequently drive surprises.

The Federal Reserve targets 2% inflation on the PCE price index rather than CPI, but CPI comes first and several components feed directly into PCE. Combined with PPI, it lets economists estimate core PCE before it’s released. A surprise in core CPI can move Treasury yields, the US dollar and equities sharply and shift rate expectations ahead of the next FOMC meeting.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Morning Kickstart. Oil slides as Waller puts a half-point hike in play. Markets brace for CPI

In the morning video above, I take a look at the three major currency pairs—EURUSD, USDJPY and GBPUSD—from a technical perspective. For each pair, I outline the bias, the risk-defining levels and the targets that would give either the buyers or sellers more control.

Crude oil is down sharply again, Treasury yields are higher, and U.S. stock futures are mixed ahead of the 8:30 AM ET CPI release. The dollar is firmer across the board, but most of the gains are modest. The Australian dollar is the weakest of the majors against the greenback, with AUDUSD down 0.30%. The New Zealand dollar is holding up best, with NZDUSD down just 0.04%.

Crude oil extends its slide as Trump plays down fresh strikes on Iran

WTI is trading at $84.90, down 2.25% after falling about 4.5% on Monday. President Trump said he would hold off on fresh strikes against Iran following appeals from regional leaders, including Qatar’s prime minister. Trump indicated the U.S. naval blockade would stay in place for now, while Tehran continued to insist on its conditions for talks, including lifting the blockade. Shipping disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz remain a risk, even as traders price in lower odds of an immediate escalation.

For oil, the next question is whether diplomacy leads to a change in shipping conditions. Another sign of progress could take more of the supply-risk premium out of crude. A fresh disruption around Hormuz could bring some of it back quickly. InvestingLive’s crude oil coverage. investinglive.com

Waller gives traders a number to watch at 8:30 AM ET

Fed Governor Christopher Waller said he would support a 25-basis-point hike in December even if October inflation cools. If core CPI rises around 0.3% month over month or higher, he said the Fed should consider 50 basis points. The consensus is 0.2%, so a one-tenth upside surprise would put the report right at the level he flagged. InvestingLive’s Waller coverage. Federal Reserve Board

Waller is concerned about how broadly prices are rising and how long higher energy costs could keep feeding through to other prices. He sees employment as close to the Fed’s goal and expects output to keep growing at a solid pace, even if growth slows this quarter. In follow-up remarks, he said he wants to reverse at least the three insurance cuts and is looking for a much smaller adjustment than 150–200 basis points. Treasuries initially sold off, stocks came under pressure and the dollar firmed on the half-point headline. Treasuries recovered a little ground after his follow-up. Federal Reserve Board

In the UK, Bank of England Deputy Governor Clare Lombardelli said further rate hikes may be needed in the near term, even with the UK labor market stuck in low gear. She described a low-hire, low-fire market and said she’s watching whether hiring picks up, workers can move into available jobs, and softer labor demand is actually easing wage and price pressures. For now, she sees inflation risks tilted to the upside. The longer energy costs stay high, the more pressure businesses face to restore margins by passing those costs on to customers. That could keep inflation sticky and make it harder to get back to the BoE’s 2% target.

The 10-year yield bounces from the 4.816% area

The U.S. 10-year yield is back up to 4.894% after trading as low as 4.814% last week. That low tested two technical levels at 4.816% in the same move. The first is the 38.2% retracement of the rise from the March 2 low to the 5.365% high. The second is the rising 100-day moving average.

That makes 4.814%–4.816% my barometer. Staying above that area keeps the rebound in yields intact. A sustained break below it would give bond buyers more control and open the door to a deeper retracement in yields. The first test is CPI. The 10-year auction gives us another read on demand this afternoon.

  • 5-year yield: 4.707%, up 4.8 basis points
  • 10-year yield: 4.894%, up 3.3 basis points
  • 30-year yield: 5.271%, up 1.5 basis points

The 2-year is leading the move higher. I’ll be watching that maturity after CPI for the clearest initial read on how traders are adjusting their December rate expectations.

Nasdaq 100 futures ease after Monday’s 3.40% rally

  • Nasdaq 100 on Monday: +3.40%, its best day since March 31, 2026, and second-best since May 12, 2025.

  • S&P 500 futures at 7:40 AM ET: +6 points
  • Nasdaq 100 futures at 7:40 AM ET: −99 points

The Dow is firmer this morning while the Nasdaq 100 is giving back some of Monday’s gain. Elsewhere, gold is down 1.54% at $4,076.92, silver is down 2.17% at $52.23 and Bitcoin is down 1.49% at $74,145.

Currency ranges ahead of CPI

Using the quoted highs and lows and the 22-day average ranges:

  • EURUSD 1.1214–1.1251, 37 pips, 57% of average
  • GBPUSD 1.3423–1.3458, 35 pips, 48% of average
  • USDJPY 157.88–158.24, 36 pips, 42% of average
  • USDCHF 0.8175–0.8211, 36 pips, 64% of average
  • USDCAD 1.4106–1.4140, 34 pips, 52% of average
  • AUDUSD 0.6907–0.6930, 23 pips, 46% of average
  • NZDUSD 0.5624–0.5649, 25 pips, 50% of average

USDJPY has covered the smallest share of its normal range. It’s also sitting near the session high with U.S. yields moving up. That makes 158.24 a good first level to watch on the CPI reaction. GBPUSD and AUDUSD have also covered less than half their normal ranges.

North American calendar

  • 8:30 AM ET – U.S. October headline CPI m/m – Forecast +0.3% – Previous +0.6%.
  • 8:30 AM ET – U.S. October core CPI m/m – Forecast +0.2% – Previous +0.3%.
  • 1:00 PM ET – U.S. Treasury 10-year note auction – $42 billion offering.

The focus is on the monthly CPI readings. The gap in October 2025 data from last year’s government shutdown means there will be no official October year-over-year comparison. investinglive.com

EURUSD, USDJPY and GBPUSD technical outlook

EURUSD is trading at 1.1215, a pip above the session low at 1.1214. Sellers have the near-term edge. A break that holds below 1.1214 would put the round 1.1200 level in focus. If the break fails and the price gets back above 1.1214, sellers lose that immediate advantage. A move above 1.1251 would give buyers more control.

USDJPY is trading at 158.20, just below the 158.24 high. Buyers have the near-term edge. A move through 158.24 that holds would put 158.50 in focus. If the break fails, I’d watch 158.00 as the first downside barometer. A move below there would bring the session low at 157.88 back into play.

GBPUSD is trading at 1.3426, near the 1.3423 low. A break below 1.3423 would give sellers more control and turn attention to 1.3400. If buyers defend the low, 1.3458 is the other side of the range and the level they need to get above to take more control.

Around CPI, I’ll watch what happens on the first retest. If USDJPY breaks 158.24 and buyers defend it on a dip, that gives them a nearby level to lean against. If the price slips back into the range, the breakout buyers have lost that level.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.
